title: Lloyds Banking Group Appoints Nigel Hinshelwood to Main Board Following PRA Direction
short: Lloyds Banking Group has announced board changes following updated ring-fencing governance arrangements allowed by the Prudential Regulation Authority, while two non-executive directors prepare to step down in 2027.
quick: Lloyds Banking Group has announced board changes following updated ring-fencing governance arrangements allowed by the Prudential Regulation Authority, while two non-executive directors prepare to step down in 2027.
lead: Lloyds Banking Group has announced board changes following updated ring-fencing governance arrangements allowed by the Prudential Regulation Authority, while two non-executive directors prepare to step down in 2027.
blocks: Board Appointment and Regulatory Framework

Lloyds Banking Group plc has announced board changes following updated ring-fencing governance arrangements allowed by the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA). A PRA Direction dated 8 May 2026 permits board members of Lloyds Bank plc and Bank of Scotland plc to serve simultaneously on the board of Lloyds Banking Group plc.
Nigel Hinshelwood's Committee Roles

Nigel Hinshelwood will join the group's board as an independent non-executive director on 1 November 2026. On the same date, he will be appointed to the group's audit, board risk, nomination and governance, and remuneration committees. Mr Hinshelwood has served as Senior Independent Director of the ring-fenced banks since 1 January 2019, attending group board and committee meetings as an observer.
Upcoming Director Departures

Lloyds also confirmed that two other non-executive directors of the ring-fenced banks, Sarah Bentley and Brendan Gilligan, will step down from their directorships on 28 February 2027 after over eight years of service. Sir Robin Budenberg, Chair of Lloyds Banking Group, thanked both outgoing directors for their long-standing service.

title: Lloyds Banking Group appoints Chris Rhodes as non-executive director
short: The former Virgin Money chief executive joins the Lloyds board with effect from 1 November 2026.
quick: The former Virgin Money chief executive joins the Lloyds board with effect from 1 November 2026.
lead: The former Virgin Money chief executive joins the Lloyds board with effect from 1 November 2026.
blocks: Board appointment details

Lloyds Banking Group plc has announced the appointment of Chris Rhodes as an independent non-executive director. Alongside his board seat, Rhodes will take up positions as a member of the Group's Audit Committee and Board Risk Committee. All appointments become effective from 1 November 2026. The group confirmed that there is no other information to be disclosed under UK Listing Rule 6.4.8R.
Banking background and career history

Rhodes brings over 30 years of UK banking industry experience to the role, having covered senior leadership positions across finance, treasury, operations, product and proposition development, and marketing. He began his career at Ernst & Whinney, a legacy firm of EY, before moving to Alliance & Leicester plc. At Alliance & Leicester he qualified as a chartered accountant and served in several roles including Interim Chief Executive Officer, Group Finance Director, Managing Director of Retail Banking, and Operations Director. He subsequently joined Nationwide Building Society, holding positions that included Chief Financial Officer, Chief Products and Proposition Officer, and Group Retail Director. Most recently, Rhodes served as Chief Executive Officer of Virgin Money until earlier this year, following its acquisition by Nationwide Building Society. Lloyds notes that he currently has no other external commitments.
Leadership commentary

Sir Robin Budenberg, Chair of Lloyds Banking Group, says that the group is delighted to welcome Rhodes to the board. Sir Robin highlights that Rhodes brings outstanding experience of the financial and regulatory management of financial institutions alongside deep retail customer knowledge.

title: TPR issues guidance on hidden AI risks in pension portfolios
short: The Pensions Regulator has urged scheme trustees to assess their total exposure to artificial intelligence, warning that even diversified funds may hold hidden concentration risks.
quick: The Pensions Regulator has urged scheme trustees to assess their total exposure to artificial intelligence, warning that even diversified funds may hold hidden concentration risks.
lead: The Pensions Regulator has urged scheme trustees to assess their total exposure to artificial intelligence, warning that even diversified funds may hold hidden concentration risks.
blocks: Identifying hidden market exposure

The Pensions Regulator (TPR) has published guidance instructing pension scheme trustees to identify and manage hidden investment exposure to artificial intelligence (AI). As AI technology spreads across multiple industries, TPR warned that even apparently diversified portfolios could contain unaccounted concentration risks. TPR says trustees should examine their whole portfolio rather than evaluating individual funds or asset classes in isolation.
Rapid expansion of AI funding

The regulator noted that investment in AI-related activities is expanding rapidly across global markets. Reports cited by TPR, including the Stanford HAI 2026 AI Index Report, show that global private AI investment rose by 127.5% year-on-year in 2025, with total global corporate AI investment more than doubling over the same period. TPR highlighted that while this expansion presents new opportunities, it also introduces specific risks for pension scheme investments.
Five key steps for scheme governance

TPR expects schemes to maintain high standards of governance across short, medium, and long-term horizons. To meet these expectations, TPR expects trustees to assess direct and indirect AI exposure across all asset classes and perform scenario testing under severe but plausible stressed market conditions. Trustees must also review whether portfolio diversification remains effective if market correlations change during a downturn, challenge investment advisers on potential market impacts, and take proportionate action based on their scheme's individual circumstances.
Regulatory call to action

Ben Gunnee, TPR's Executive Director of Market Oversight, stated that trustees need to assess their exposure, test portfolio resilience, and question their advisers now. He stressed that schemes must understand how market developments could affect their investments under different market conditions.

A risk management practice used to test portfolio resilience under severe hypothetical market conditions.

title: Standard Life study finds friction hampers customer pension understanding
short: Three years of behavioural science research by Standard Life indicates that avoidable complexity and effort can stop customers from understanding key pension decisions.
quick: Three years of behavioural science research by Standard Life indicates that avoidable complexity and effort can stop customers from understanding key pension decisions.
lead: Three years of behavioural science research by Standard Life indicates that avoidable complexity and effort can stop customers from understanding key pension decisions.
blocks: Friction creates barriers to decision-making

A three-year analysis of customer behaviour by Standard Life found that customer understanding is less likely to fail because information is missing, and more likely to break down when avoidable friction, uncertainty and complexity make it harder to identify what matters and what to do next. The provider's "Understanding Under Pressure" report gathers behavioural science research, customer testing, experimentation and journey analysis. Standard Life notes that these barriers, sometimes known as sludge, can be particularly significant for customers experiencing vulnerable circumstances such as bereavement, poor health, financial pressure or major life events.
High clarity ratings mask gaps in comprehension

The research highlights a distinction between whether a communication is perceived as clear and whether customers can successfully use it to make informed decisions. In one test cited in the report, participants gave a pension withdrawal communication an average clarity rating of 4.3 out of 5. However, when asked to explain what could happen to the portion of their pension that remained invested after taking a withdrawal, only 40% were able to do so. Standard Life notes this presents a challenge under Consumer Duty regulations, where delivering good customer outcomes depends on customers being able to understand and act on information in practice.
Redesigned journeys reduce inbound queries

To help firms assess customer communications, Standard Life created a four-question framework focusing on where to start, why it matters, what to notice and what to do next. In a live randomised controlled trial of redesigned pension withdrawal communications, customers using the revised materials were 2.5 times more likely to complete the process. Inbound calls fell from 40% to 24%, while requests for further information reduced from 18% to 5%. In a separate redesign of its online bereavement notification service, more than 80% of customers successfully uploaded a death certificate during their first interaction.

title: Arbuthnot Banking Group lifts profit expectations on strong lending and wealth growth
short: The banking group reports positive third-quarter performance across its loan books and wealth management division, leading the board to anticipate higher full-year profit.
quick: The banking group reports positive third-quarter performance across its loan books and wealth management division, leading the board to anticipate higher full-year profit.
lead: The banking group reports positive third-quarter performance across its loan books and wealth management division, leading the board to anticipate higher full-year profit.
blocks: Trading Performance and Profit Outlook

Arbuthnot Banking Group PLC has announced that its board expects full-year profit before tax for 2026 to come in ahead of prior expectations. The group points to ongoing loan book growth across the first nine months of the year, a stable interest rate environment, and continued momentum within its wealth management business as the main drivers behind this upgrade.
Lending and Deposit Figures

Customer loans and leased assets reached two point five billion pounds at the thirty-first of September period end, marking a twelve percent increase over the preceding twelve months. Customer deposit balances finished the period at four point nine billion pounds, reflecting a ten percent rise year-on-year and a two percent increase during the third quarter alone. Specialist lending divisions performed particularly strongly, delivering twenty-six percent growth over the past twelve months.
Wealth Management Expansion

Funds under Management and Administration grew to three point zero nine billion pounds by the end of September, up fifteen percent from the start of the year and twenty-one percent higher than the same point in twenty-twenty-five. The wealth management unit turned a net profit for the quarter, aided by fees and commission from wealth planning advising clients.
